summary: An invite becomes an account of the kind the invite names: a vault owner sets up a vault in the browser before anything is sent, an administrator runs the identical derivation and discards the Master Key, and one transaction writes the principal, its password credential, a wrapper and profile record where they apply, and the invite's consumption.

read.role: the rule by which registration starts its session

sections: Bootstrap: the first administrator, and the locked-out one
read.role: the invite row this consumes, its kind, and the generic refusal every bad invite shares
the validator the profile record is written through
the payload shape whose two required keys registration writes
the kind: currency rows that are the whole of the main-currency list
the schema this writes into, the headers the page is served with, and the Public group that GET /register and POST /api/register belong to, which the gate passes with no session
the form, input and progress conventions, and the fact that the unauthenticated screens sit outside the shell
the two forms the invite's kind chooses between

page.value: GET /register?invite=<token>, server-rendered Jinja, embedding the server's current default KDF envelope and, for a vault owner invite, the currency half of the symbol table. An invalid token renders an error page with no form

formIsChosenByTheInvite.value: the rendered form is the one the invite's kind calls for. An administrator invite renders no currency picker and states on the page that this link creates an administrator account with no vault. Nothing on either form lets the person choose the kind

endpoint.value: POST /api/register with invite token, username, Auth Key, salt and KDF parameter envelope, plus, for a vault owner, wrapped DEK and its nonce and the profile record's id, schema version, ciphertext and nonce

payloadIsCheckedAgainstTheInvite.value: the invite row's kind is the discriminator. A payload carrying a wrapper or a profile record against an administrator invite is a Bad Request, and one omitting them against a vault owner invite is too. Nothing in the request names a kind

kdfParameters.value: Argon2id at 64 MiB memory, 3 iterations, parallelism 1, over a 128-bit salt, via the argon2id library (npm argon2id, from openpgpjs), HKDF-split into Master Key and Auth Key

saltSize.value: a random 128-bit salt from crypto.getRandomValues, validated server-side as exactly 16 bytes

dekSize.value: a random 256-bit DEK, wrapped under the Master Key with AES-256-GCM

administratorDerivation.value: the same salt generation, the same Argon2id at the same parameters, and the same HKDF split, after which the Master Key is discarded. No DEK, no wrapper, no profile record, no main currency

initialProfilePayload.value: { mainCurrency, createdAt }, the two required keys of the profile payload. The optional ones are written later by the settings that own them

profileAad.value: account_id empty, record_type profile, its own record_id, its own schema_version, version 1, built entirely before the request is sent because principal_id is not part of the AAD

tablesWritten.value: principals takes identity and kind only, meaning the normalized username, the kind copied from the invite, and the two timestamps, and no key column. credentials takes exactly one row with method 'password' for both kinds, its params holding the request's salt and KDF envelope verbatim and its verifier the Argon2id hash of the submitted Auth Key. dek_wrappers takes exactly one row for a vault owner and none at all for an administrator

onePasswordCredential.value: enforced by a unique index on principal_id restricted to method = 'password', written in the same transaction as the principal row

methodIsNotClientInput.value: the server writes 'password' and no endpoint in v1 accepts any other value, so a payload carrying a method field is a Bad Request

kindIsNotClientInput.value: the server copies kind from the invite row and no endpoint anywhere writes it again. A payload carrying a kind field of any value is rejected

registrationSession.value: the session starts by the same rule as a sign-in. The account is new, so the carried session is at most another account's, and a live one is deleted and replaced. A failed registration leaves the carried session working

oneTransaction.value: the principal row, its password credential row, its wrapper and profile record where they apply, and the invite's consumption commit together or not at all

passwordPolicy.value: at least 12 characters and a zxcvbn score of at least 3, no composition rules. Client-enforced by construction, because the server never sees the password

noRecoveryAcknowledgement.value: the screen states plainly that there is no password recovery and requires an explicit acknowledgement before submitting. The administrator form carries none and claims nothing about recovery in its place

usernameRules.value: normalized by trimming and lowercasing before storage and comparison, 3 to 32 characters of [a-z0-9._-], unique across one namespace covering both kinds. The reserved sentinel system:bootstrap is refused as a username

serverValidation.value: salt exactly 16 bytes, KDF envelope parameters at or above the server's configured minimum, and wrapped DEK and profile blobs within the blob and quota limits

mainCurrencyList.value: exactly the kind: currency rows of the operator's symbol table, seeded from the FX provider's own currency list. Not the full ISO 4217 set

mainCurrencyStorage.value: only inside the encrypted profile record, never as a plaintext column

enumerationIsAcceptedHere.value: a taken username is reported clearly. Username enumeration at registration is accepted rather than defended, because the endpoint is invite-gated. The refusal is the same whichever kind holds the name, so the attempt reveals existence but not kind

noWeakFallback.value: a client that cannot run WASM Argon2id fails hard with no weaker fallback KDF, for both kinds. A client that can run WASM but cannot allocate the KDF's memory gets a distinct hard failure naming the moment rather than the device, with a retry and no vault created, and must not fall back to weaker parameters

derivationRunsInAWorker.value: run derivation in a Web Worker so the UI thread stays responsive, with a busy state

fixtures: a valid unused vault owner invite and a valid unused administrator invite
an invalid, an expired, a used and a revoked invite, for the byte-identical error assertion shared with admin-invites
request-payload capture over the whole registration flow, for the assertion that no password, Master Key or unwrapped DEK is sent

a hand-built POST /api/register carrying a kind field, a method field, a wrapper against an administrator invite, a missing wrapper against a vault owner invite, KDF parameters below the server minimum, and a salt that is not 16 bytes
a fault injected into the profile insert, for the all-or-nothing assertion including the unconsumed invite
a seeded account of each kind holding the same username, for the cross-kind collision refusal
an account registered through PUT /api/records with an equivalent profile record, for the indistinguishability assertion
another account's live session cookie, carried into a successful and into a failed registration
focus: the administrator path must leave zero dek_wrappers rows and zero records rows, asserted against both tables rather than against the response. Zero is the whole guarantee and an implementation that writes an empty wrapper row passes every behaviour test

the principals row must hold no salt, no KDF envelope, no Auth Key hash and no wrapped DEK, asserted against the table's full column set so the test fails if one is added back. Asserting the values are absent is not the same as asserting the columns are

the profile AAD must be shown to be built entirely before the request is sent, by encrypting the blob in a test with no server interaction at all. A test that checks the AAD after a successful registration cannot tell whether the client waited for an identity

a below-minimum KDF envelope must be rejected server-side even though the client UI would never send one. This is the case only a hand-built request reaches, and it is the one that decides whether the rule is a control or a convention
the request payload assertion has to run against the captured bytes, not against an inspection of the code, and it has to cover the password, the Master Key and the unwrapped DEK separately
the four bad-invite responses must be byte-identical, not merely similar in wording. Any difference in length, ordering or status turns the page into an oracle

the profile record written by registration must be indistinguishable from one written through PUT /api/records: same validation, same column values, same AAD. A second record writer that happens to produce the same columns today is exactly what this criterion exists to prevent
a registration that fails partway must leave the invite unconsumed, asserted against the invite row and not only against the absence of the account

a registration carrying another account's live cookie must delete that sessions row, asserted against the table, and the old cookie must answer Unauthorized. A failed registration must leave the carried session working
